claim: House sparrows (Passer domesticus) inhabit most human-modified habitats of the globe from the northernmost tip of Scandinavia to the southernmost corner of Patagonia, across six continents.
source: From the northernmost tip of Scandinavia to the southernmost corner of Patagonia, and across six continents, house sparrows (Passer domesticus) inhabit most human-modified habitats of the globe.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the geographic distribution of house sparrows, presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Over 7,000 articles have been published on house sparrows.
source: With over 7,000 articles published, the species has become a workhorse for not only the study of self-urbanized wildlife, but also for understanding life history and body size evolution, sexual selection and many other biological phenomena.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the volume of scientific literature on house sparrows, presented as factual data.

claim: House sparrows have become a workhorse for the study of self-urbanized wildlife.
source: With over 7,000 articles published, the species has become a workhorse for not only the study of self-urbanized wildlife, but also for understanding life history and body size evolution, sexual selection and many other biological phenomena.
evidence: This claim is supported by the large volume of published research (over 7,000 articles) mentioned in the same sentence.

claim: House sparrows are used for understanding life history and body size evolution.
source: With over 7,000 articles published, the species has become a workhorse for not only the study of self-urbanized wildlife, but also for understanding life history and body size evolution, sexual selection and many other biological phenomena.
evidence: This is supported by the extensive literature on the species and is presented as established knowledge.

claim: House sparrows are used for understanding sexual selection.
source: With over 7,000 articles published, the species has become a workhorse for not only the study of self-urbanized wildlife, but also for understanding life history and body size evolution, sexual selection and many other biological phenomena.
evidence: This is supported by the extensive literature on the species and is presented as established knowledge.

claim: House sparrows are small, sexually dimorphic birds in the family Passeridae.
source: House sparrows are small, sexually dimorphic birds in the family Passeridae.
evidence: This is a taxonomic and morphological description based on established biological knowledge.

claim: The house sparrow species is represented by 12 different subspecies.
source: The species is one of the most widely distributed and common birds in the world, represented by 12 different subspecies (Summers-Smith, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 2009.

claim: House sparrows can be found living and breeding in climatically extreme environments from deserts in southern California to cities above the Arctic circle.
source: House sparrows can be found living and breeding in climactically extreme environments from deserts in southern California to cities above the Arctic circle, where they are found almost exclusively in close proximity to human habitation (Hanson et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hanson et al., 2020b.

claim: House sparrows are found almost exclusively in close proximity to human habitation.
source: House sparrows can be found living and breeding in climactically extreme environments from deserts in southern California to cities above the Arctic circle, where they are found almost exclusively in close proximity to human habitation (Hanson et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hanson et al., 2020b.

claim: House sparrows are considered anthrodependent.
source: Considered anthrodependent, some populations have gone extinct locally without human presence (Ravinet et al., 2018; Summers-Smith, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ravinet et al., 2018 and Summers-Smith, 1988, and is further evidenced by the observation that some populations have gone extinct without human presence.

claim: Some house sparrow populations have gone extinct locally without human presence.
source: Considered anthrodependent, some populations have gone extinct locally without human presence (Ravinet et al., 2018; Summers-Smith, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ravinet et al., 2018 and Summers-Smith, 1988.

claim: House sparrows received their species identifier 'domesticus' from Carl Linnaeus in 1758.
source: It is for this relationship with people that they received their species identifier domesticus, which derives from the Latin domus or 'house', from Carl Linnaeus in 1758 (Jobling, 2009; Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jobling, 2009 and Anderson, 2006.

claim: The species identifier 'domesticus' derives from the Latin 'domus' or 'house'.
source: It is for this relationship with people that they received their species identifier domesticus, which derives from the Latin domus or 'house', from Carl Linnaeus in 1758 (Jobling, 2009; Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jobling, 2009 and Anderson, 2006.

claim: House sparrows are native to parts of Asia, North Africa and most of Europe.
source: House sparrows are native to parts of Asia, North Africa and most of Europe, (with the exception of Italy which is occupied by the Italian sparrow P. italiae; Animation 1).
evidence: This claim is presented as established knowledge and is supported by reference to Animation 1.

claim: Italy is occupied by the Italian sparrow P. italiae rather than house sparrows.
source: House sparrows are native to parts of Asia, North Africa and most of Europe, (with the exception of Italy which is occupied by the Italian sparrow P. italiae; Animation 1).
evidence: This claim is presented as established knowledge and is supported by reference to Animation 1.

claim: House sparrows became commensal some 10,000 years ago.
source: Becoming commensal some 10,000 years ago, house sparrows are now strongly associated with habitats that have been modified by humans.
evidence: This is a historical claim presented as established knowledge about the species' relationship with humans.

claim: House sparrows are now strongly associated with habitats that have been modified by humans.
source: Becoming commensal some 10,000 years ago, house sparrows are now strongly associated with habitats that have been modified by humans.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the species' current habitat preferences.

claim: House sparrows continue to increase their geographic range by exploiting ongoing and accelerating anthropogenic change.
source: However, they also continue to increase their geographic range by exploiting ongoing and accelerating anthropogenic change (Ravinet et al., 2018; Saetre et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ravinet et al., 2018 and Saetre et al., 2012.

claim: House sparrows colonized Northern Europe, Eastern Europe and Central Asia in the early 1800s as agriculture spread and urbanization increased.
source: A reliance on humans is evident from their colonization of Northern Europe, Eastern Europe and Central Asia in the early 1800s, as agriculture spread and urbanization increased (Summers-Smith, 1963).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1963.

claim: Significant declines in house sparrow populations have been reported in the native range of the species since the 1970s.
source: Though still widespread, significant declines have been reported in the native range of the species since the 1970s.
evidence: This claim is presented as an observation and is further supported by citations in the following sentence.

claim: House sparrow declines in their native range have been attributed to infectious disease, pollution, pesticide use, predator dynamics, new building methodologies and more efficient grain harvesting and storage.
source: This topic remains contentious (Box 1), but these declines have been attributed to a multitude of factors, including infectious disease, pollution, pesticide use, predator dynamics, new building methodologies and more efficient grain harvesting and storage (Shaw et al., 2008; Summers-Smith, 2003; Singh et al., 2013; Bell et al., 2010; Dadam et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shaw et al., 2008; Summers-Smith, 2003; Singh et al., 2013; Bell et al., 2010; Dadam et al., 2019.

claim: House sparrows are one of the most ubiquitous birds in the world.
source: House sparrows are one of the most ubiquitous birds in the world (Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claim: In approximately 170 years, house sparrows colonized the globe such that they now reside in every continent except Antarctica.
source: In approximately 170 years, they colonized the globe such that they now reside in every continent except Antarctica and occupy an estimated 76,600,000 km2 (Birdlife international, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Birdlife international, 2018.

claim: House sparrows occupy an estimated 76,600,000 km2.
source: In approximately 170 years, they colonized the globe such that they now reside in every continent except Antarctica and occupy an estimated 76,600,000 km2 (Birdlife international, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Birdlife international, 2018.

claim: There have been over 250 introduction or translocation events of house sparrows recorded worldwide.
source: There have been over 250 introduction or translocation events recorded worldwide (Table 1), with the first deliberate successful introduction occurring in 1851 in New York City (Summers-Smith, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Table 1 and a citation to Summers-Smith, 1988.

claim: The first deliberate successful introduction of house sparrows occurred in 1851 in New York City.
source: There have been over 250 introduction or translocation events recorded worldwide (Table 1), with the first deliberate successful introduction occurring in 1851 in New York City (Summers-Smith, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1988.

claim: Many house sparrow introductions stemmed from colonial acclimatization societies purposefully releasing birds for cultural reasons or as failed attempts at biological control.
source: Many introductions stemmed from colonial acclimatization societies purposefully releasing birds for cultural reasons or as failed attempts at biological control.
evidence: This is presented as historical knowledge about the reasons for house sparrow introductions.

claim: Recent house sparrow introductions have been accidental.
source: More recently, introductions have been accidental.
evidence: This is presented as a general observation about recent introduction patterns.

claim: Ship-assisted dispersal of house sparrows has been documented.
source: Ship-assisted dispersal (e.g., cargo ships, cruise liners) has been documented, and other types of vehicle-assisted dispersal are also likely (Sainz‐Borgo et al., 2016; Schrey et al., 2014; Clergeau et al., 2004; Szent-Ivány, 1959; Summers-Smith, 1963).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sainz‐Borgo et al., 2016; Schrey et al., 2014; Clergeau et al., 2004; Szent-Ivány, 1959; Summers-Smith, 1963.

claim: Other types of vehicle-assisted dispersal of house sparrows are likely.
source: Ship-assisted dispersal (e.g., cargo ships, cruise liners) has been documented, and other types of vehicle-assisted dispersal are also likely (Sainz‐Borgo et al., 2016; Schrey et al., 2014; Clergeau et al., 2004; Szent-Ivány, 1959; Summers-Smith, 1963).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from documented ship-assisted dispersal, supported by the same citations.

claim: Male house sparrows tend to be heavier and larger than females.
source: Male house sparrows tend to be heavier and larger than females (Figure 1; Hanson et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and a citation to Hanson et al., 2020b.

claim: Male house sparrows have gray crests and black post-ocular stripes with conspicuous white spots behind the eyes.
source: Males have gray crests and black post-ocular stripes with conspicuous white spots behind the eyes (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a morphological description supported by reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Male house sparrow abdomens are gray whereas bills, tails, wings and body feathers are black or dark brown.
source: Male abdomens are gray whereas bills, tails, wings and body feathers are black or dark brown.
evidence: This is a morphological description presented as established knowledge.

claim: Female house sparrow plumage is drabber than male plumage, with crests that are dark brown and post-ocular stripes that are light brown.
source: Plumage in females is drabber, with crests that are dark brown and post-ocular stripes that are light brown.
evidence: This is a morphological description presented as established knowledge.

claim: Female house sparrows lack black head markings and have gray-brown to light brown cheeks, bills and feathers.
source: Females lack black head markings and have gray-brown to light brown cheeks, bills and feathers (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a morphological description supported by reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Female house sparrow plumage resembles juveniles and females from other Passer species so much that distinguishing them visually is often difficult.
source: Female plumage resembles juveniles and females from other Passer species so much that distinguishing them visually is often difficult (Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claim: House sparrow subspecies differ in size, mass and male plumage.
source: Subspecies also differ in size, mass and male plumage (See Summers-Smith, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1988.

claim: The most conspicuous morphological difference between male and female house sparrows is the large black throat badge of males.
source: The most conspicuous morphological difference between male and female sparrows is the large black throat badge of males.
evidence: This is a morphological observation presented as established knowledge.

claim: The male house sparrow throat badge is one of the factors that made this species a model in behavioral ecology.
source: Arguably, this badge is one of the factors that made this species a model in behavioral ecology (Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018.

claim: Large badge size in male house sparrows has been thought to convey an individual's propensity to win in male-male competitive interactions.
source: Large badge size has been thought to convey an individual's propensity to win in male-male competitive interactions; the logic was that possessing information a priori about a competitor could save both the badge-holder and his opponents from wasted energy and risk of injury (Rohwer, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rohwer, 1975.

claim: The largest meta-analysis to date revealed that badge size in male house sparrows is at best an unreliable signal of dominance status.
source: Recently, however, the largest meta-analysis to date revealed that badge size is at best an unreliable signal of dominance status (Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018.

claim: The currently favored hypothesis for male house sparrow badge size is that it serves some role in mate choice.
source: The currently favored hypothesis for badge size is that it serves some role in mate choice, as females tend to choose males with large badges, and badge size is positively correlated with male sexual behaviors (Veiga, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Veiga, 1996.

claim: Female house sparrows tend to choose males with large badges.
source: The currently favored hypothesis for badge size is that it serves some role in mate choice, as females tend to choose males with large badges, and badge size is positively correlated with male sexual behaviors (Veiga, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Veiga, 1996.

claim: Badge size in male house sparrows is positively correlated with male sexual behaviors.
source: The currently favored hypothesis for badge size is that it serves some role in mate choice, as females tend to choose males with large badges, and badge size is positively correlated with male sexual behaviors (Veiga, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Veiga, 1996.

claim: Many morphological characteristics of house sparrows vary geographically.
source: Importantly, many morphological characteristics also vary geographically.
evidence: This is a general observation that is elaborated with specific examples and citations in subsequent sentences.

claim: Plumage color and aspects of body size (wing, tail and tarsus length, skeletal characteristics, and body mass) were found to vary within and between native and introduced house sparrow populations.
source: Most well-known through the pioneering work of Richard F Johnston and Robert K Selander, plumage color and aspects of body size (wing, tail and tarsus length, skeletal characteristics, and body mass) were found to vary within and between native and introduced populations (Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1964; Johnston and Selander, 1971; Johnston, 1969; Johnston, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1964; Johnston and Selander, 1971; Johnston, 1969; Johnston, 1973.

claim: Introduced house sparrow populations in North America have pale coloration in hot, arid climates, but darker coloration in cooler, humid climates.
source: Introduced populations in North America were discovered to have pale coloration in hot, arid climates, but darker coloration in cooler, humid climates (Johnston and Selander, 1964).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Johnston and Selander, 1964.

claim: Body size of house sparrows increased with latitude.
source: Body size of birds also increased with latitude, and perhaps most interestingly, all of these geographic trends in biological traits arose rapidly in the introduced populations (Johnston and Selander, 1964; Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnston and Selander, 1964; Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1971.

claim: Geographic trends in biological traits of house sparrows arose rapidly in the introduced populations.
source: Body size of birds also increased with latitude, and perhaps most interestingly, all of these geographic trends in biological traits arose rapidly in the introduced populations (Johnston and Selander, 1964; Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnston and Selander, 1964; Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1971.

claim: Nestling house sparrows are fed an insect-based diet for the first three days after hatching.
source: Nestling house sparrows are fed an insect-based diet for the first three days after hatching.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about house sparrow feeding behavior.

claim: After fledging, house sparrows favor grains, especially outside urban areas.
source: Later, following fledging, they favor grains, especially outside urban areas (Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claim: Adult house sparrows have a fairly opportunistic diet throughout much of the year, especially in cities and suburbs where human refuse is plentiful.
source: Adult house sparrows have a fairly opportunistic diet throughout much of the year, especially in cities and suburbs where human refuse is plentiful (Summers-Smith, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1988.

claim: Plasticity in the release of digestive enzymes might be one reason house sparrows are adept at exploiting diverse diets.
source: One of the reasons house sparrows are so adept at exploiting diverse diets might involve plasticity in the release of digestive enzymes (Brzek et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to Brzek et al., 2009.

claim: House sparrows in the roughly 40-year-old Panama population consume unfamiliar foods more quickly than birds from a much older invasive population in New Jersey in the United States.
source: For example, house sparrows in the roughly 40-year-old Panama population consume unfamiliar foods more quickly than birds from a much older invasive population in New Jersey in the United States (Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005.

claim: Kenyan house sparrows living at the expanding range edge approach and eat novel foods more quickly than birds from the core of the population.
source: A similar pattern is observed among Kenyan sparrows such that birds living at the expanding range edge of that colonization approach and eat novel foods more quickly than birds from the core of the population (Liebl and Martin, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liebl and Martin, 2014.

claim: A tendency to eat novel foods may benefit house sparrows in habitats where resources are scarce or unfamiliar.
source: A tendency to eat novel foods may benefit birds in habitats where resources are scarce or unfamiliar, but such behavior could also come with risks.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on logical inference about the adaptive value of behavioral traits.

claim: Eating novel foods could expose house sparrows to risks such as spoiled foods or novel toxins that may activate the immune system.
source: Spoiled foods or exposure to novel toxins, for example, may activate the immune system (Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005.

claim: House sparrow populations differ extensively in how their immune systems are organized and what parasites they harbor throughout their lives.
source: This notion is supported by the observation that populations differ quite extensively in how their immune systems are organized and what parasites they harbor throughout their lives (Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2014; Coon and Martin, 2014; Coon et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2014; Coon and Martin, 2014; Coon et al., 2014.

claim: House sparrows tend to build nests in pre-existing cavities.
source: Sparrows tend to build nests in pre-existing cavities, but they also routinely nest in roofs, eaves and walls of human-built structures (Figure 1c) as well as in densely branched trees and shrubs (Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017, and reference to Figure 1c.

claim: House sparrows routinely nest in roofs, eaves and walls of human-built structures.
source: Sparrows tend to build nests in pre-existing cavities, but they also routinely nest in roofs, eaves and walls of human-built structures (Figure 1c) as well as in densely branched trees and shrubs (Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017, and reference to Figure 1c.

claim: House sparrows nest in densely branched trees and shrubs.
source: Sparrows tend to build nests in pre-existing cavities, but they also routinely nest in roofs, eaves and walls of human-built structures (Figure 1c) as well as in densely branched trees and shrubs (Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017.

claim: House sparrow nests are comprised mostly of vegetation but some clay, sand, cloth and even dung may be used.
source: Nests are comprised mostly of vegetation but some clay, sand, cloth and even dung may be used (Heij, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heij, 1986.

claim: In some cities, house sparrow nests contain aromatic plants or cigarette butts that contain antiparasitic secondary compounds.
source: In some cities, nests also contain aromatic plants or even cigarette butts that contain antiparasitic secondary compounds (Sengupta and Shrilata, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sengupta and Shrilata, 1997.

claim: Male house sparrows initially choose nesting sites and subsequently advertise for mates by vocal and visual displays.
source: Males initially choose nesting sites and subsequently advertise for mates by vocal and visual displays (Summers-Smith, 1963).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1963.

claim: Unlike many songbirds, male house sparrows exhibit aggressive, territorial behavior only in a very small area around the nest site.
source: However, unlike many songbirds, males exhibit aggressive, territorial behavior only in a very small area around the nest site.
evidence: This is a comparative behavioral observation presented as established knowledge.

claim: Female house sparrows select males based on visual and vocal displays and the location of nest sites.
source: Females select males based on visual and vocal displays and the location of nest sites (Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claim: Once paired, male and female house sparrows often remain together for the entire season or even multiple years.
source: Once paired, males and females often remain together for the entire season or even multiple years.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about house sparrow pair bonding behavior.

claim: House sparrow pairs commonly use the same nest site for several years.
source: Pairs also commonly use the same nest site for several years (Summers-Smith, 1963), however, as is typical in most bird species, males are more likely to stay in, or habitually return to, the area around a nest site than females (Morrison et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1963.

claim: Male house sparrows are more likely to stay in, or habitually return to, the area around a nest site than females.
source: Pairs also commonly use the same nest site for several years (Summers-Smith, 1963), however, as is typical in most bird species, males are more likely to stay in, or habitually return to, the area around a nest site than females (Morrison et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morrison et al., 2008.

claim: Both male and female house sparrows defend the nest, brood the eggs and care for the young.
source: Both sexes defend the nest, brood the eggs and care for the young, though females put more effort into the brooding than males (Figure 1d; Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006 and reference to Figure 1d.

claim: Female house sparrows put more effort into brooding than males.
source: Both sexes defend the nest, brood the eggs and care for the young, though females put more effort into the brooding than males (Figure 1d; Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006 and reference to Figure 1d.

claim: House sparrow pairs are socially monogamous.
source: Pairs are socially monogamous, however, the proportion of offspring that are fathered by an extra-pair male (extra-pair paternity) can reach 26%, particularly if food is scarce and the environment is harsh (Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about house sparrow mating systems.

claim: The proportion of house sparrow offspring fathered by an extra-pair male can reach 26%, particularly if food is scarce and the environment is harsh.
source: Pairs are socially monogamous, however, the proportion of offspring that are fathered by an extra-pair male (extra-pair paternity) can reach 26%, particularly if food is scarce and the environment is harsh (Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stewart et al., 2015.

claim: House sparrows typically begin breeding during the first year of life.
source: House sparrows typically begin breeding during the first year of life, but breeding success is comparatively low in younger breeders (Hatch and Westneat, 2007).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about house sparrow life history.

claim: Breeding success is comparatively low in younger house sparrow breeders.
source: House sparrows typically begin breeding during the first year of life, but breeding success is comparatively low in younger breeders (Hatch and Westneat, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hatch and Westneat, 2007.

claim: Towards the global poles, house sparrows rely on changes in the number of hours of daylight and temperature to ensure that breeding coincides with peak food availability.
source: Towards the global poles, house sparrows, like other species, rely on changes in the number of hours of daylight and temperature to ensure that breeding coincides with peak food availability (Hau, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hau, 2001.

claim: Near the equator, both light levels and temperature are fairly stable year-round.
source: Nearer to the equator, however, both light levels and temperature are fairly stable year-round (Hau et al., 1998), and house sparrows in this region seem to use changes in precipitation regimes to time breeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hau et al., 1998.

claim: House sparrows near the equator seem to use changes in precipitation regimes to time breeding.
source: Nearer to the equator, however, both light levels and temperature are fairly stable year-round (Hau et al., 1998), and house sparrows in this region seem to use changes in precipitation regimes to time breeding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that light and temperature are stable near the equator, supported by the citation to Hau et al., 1998.

claim: In Panama, India and Malawi, house sparrows breed predominantly during the dry parts of the year.
source: In Panama, India and Malawi, for instance, house sparrows breed predominantly during the dry parts of the year, but in Zambia, sparrows breed both five months prior to the peak of the rains, and again when the rains are ongoing (Nhlane, 2000; Hanson et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nhlane, 2000 and Hanson et al., 2020b.

claim: In Zambia, house sparrows breed both five months prior to the peak of the rains, and again when the rains are ongoing.
source: In Panama, India and Malawi, for instance, house sparrows breed predominantly during the dry parts of the year, but in Zambia, sparrows breed both five months prior to the peak of the rains, and again when the rains are ongoing (Nhlane, 2000; Hanson et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nhlane, 2000 and Hanson et al., 2020b.

claim: House sparrows show clinal variation in life history and associated physiological traits along gradients in their geographic range.
source: Perhaps the main reason that house sparrows have been a model organism in basic ornithology involves the variation they show in life history and associated physiological traits along gradients in their geographic range.
evidence: This is presented as a general observation that is elaborated with specific examples in subsequent sentences.

claim: Clinal variation in house sparrows has been documented for metabolic rates.
source: Known as clinal variation, in house sparrows, this phenomenon has been documented for metabolic rates (Hudson and Kimzey, 1966; Kendeigh and Blem, 1974; Blem, 1973), hormone regulation (Romero et al., 2006; Breuner and Orchinik, 2001; Liebl and Martin, 2012), and immune defenses (Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005; Martin et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hudson and Kimzey, 1966; Kendeigh and Blem, 1974; Blem, 1973.

claim: Clinal variation in house sparrows has been documented for hormone regulation.
source: Known as clinal variation, in house sparrows, this phenomenon has been documented for metabolic rates (Hudson and Kimzey, 1966; Kendeigh and Blem, 1974; Blem, 1973), hormone regulation (Romero et al., 2006; Breuner and Orchinik, 2001; Liebl and Martin, 2012), and immune defenses (Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005; Martin et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Romero et al., 2006; Breuner and Orchinik, 2001; Liebl and Martin, 2012.

claim: Clinal variation in house sparrows has been documented for immune defenses.
source: Known as clinal variation, in house sparrows, this phenomenon has been documented for metabolic rates (Hudson and Kimzey, 1966; Kendeigh and Blem, 1974; Blem, 1973), hormone regulation (Romero et al., 2006; Breuner and Orchinik, 2001; Liebl and Martin, 2012), and immune defenses (Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005; Martin et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005; Martin et al., 2004.

claim: House sparrow clutches are small near the equator and increase pole-ward.
source: These trends are best-reflected by clinal variation in clutch size; just as in most songbirds, house sparrow clutches are small near the equator and increase pole-ward (Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claim: The pattern of clutch size variation exists in both the native and non-native distribution of house sparrows.
source: This pattern, which exists in both the native and non-native distribution, is intriguing because of the recency of most introductions.
evidence: This is presented as an observation about the geographic pattern of clutch size variation.

claim: The recency of most house sparrow introductions means that new populations would have had little time for genetic adaptation.
source: Such recency means that new populations would have had little time for genetic adaptation as well as being exposed to founder effects and other genetic challenges (i.e., bottlenecks) inherent to introductions (Baker, 1995; Lowther, 1977).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Baker, 1995 and Lowther, 1977.

claim: New house sparrow populations have been exposed to founder effects and other genetic challenges inherent to introductions.
source: Such recency means that new populations would have had little time for genetic adaptation as well as being exposed to founder effects and other genetic challenges (i.e., bottlenecks) inherent to introductions (Baker, 1995; Lowther, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baker, 1995 and Lowther, 1977.

claim: Early studies using allozymes revealed little genetic variation among and within North American house sparrow populations.
